I learned modes wrong at 19, from a man in a Sauchiehall Street guitar shop who said "Dorian is just C major starting on D". True and useless. This is the version that actually helps on a gig: each mode as its own colour, with the one note that gives it away.

## The parent scale trick (and why it's not enough)

Yes, all seven modes of C major share the same notes. But over a D minor vamp, D Dorian doesn't sound like C major at all, because the ear hears D as home. Think of modes as altered major or minor scales instead:

- Major family: Ionian (plain major), Lydian (#4), Mixolydian (b7)
- Minor family: Aeolian (plain minor), Dorian (natural 6), Phrygian (b2), Locrian (b2 and b5)

## Ionian

Plain major. Nothing to say. Most of the pop sessions I do never leave it.

## Dorian

Minor with a natural 6th. The 6th is the bright note in a dark scale. Santana, "So What" (Miles Davis, 1959), half of the funk I play on. Over Am7 - D7 the F# is the colour note. Practice: hold an A drone, play the 6th (F#) on strong beats until it stops sounding wrong.

## Phrygian

Minor with a flat 2nd. Spanish, menacing, metal. In flamenco the related scale with a major 3rd (Phrygian dominant) is everywhere, see [[Flamenco compás]]. E Phrygian over an E chord with a F on top is the sound of a bad thing about to happen in a film.

## Lydian

Major with a sharp 4th. Floating, dreamy, film-score wonder. Joe Satriani's "Flying in a Blue Dream" (1989). In F Lydian the B natural does it. The Simpsons theme is Lydian too, which ruins it a bit.

## Mixolydian

Major with a flat 7th. Rock, Celtic, bagpipe-adjacent. The Highland pipes' scale sits close enough that every Scottish folk rock song lands here. G Mixolydian over G - F - C, see [[Chord progressions]].

## Aeolian

Natural minor. Sad pop ballads. The difference from Dorian is one note (b6 against natural 6) and that one note is the difference between "Stairway" and "Oye Como Va".

## Locrian

Diminished home chord. Basically unusable as a key centre. Good for one bar of tension in a horror cue. I wrote a 30-second Locrian sting for the film club (Strathbungo Film Society) Halloween screening of "The Wicker Man" (1973) on 31 October 2024 and people laughed, which was not the plan.

## Brightest to darkest

Lydian, Ionian, Mixolydian, Dorian, Aeolian, Phrygian, Locrian. Each step flattens one more note. Learned this order from Morag Quigley and it's the single most useful thing in this note. Play C Lydian through C Locrian back to back, same root, and you hear the light go out.

## Practice plan, spring 2025

- One mode a week over a drone at 60 BPM, 10 minutes.
- Find one tune per mode by ear (see [[Ear training]]).
- Write a 16-bar tune in each mode by June. Done: Dorian, Mixolydian. Lydian one is half finished and sounds like a car advert.
